lesson.title: Debugging with print(): Your First and Fastest Diagnostic Tool
lesson.summary: Print debugging means inserting print statements at key points in code to make hidden variable values and control flow visible during a run.
lesson.body:
The most direct way to see what a running program is actually doing is to ask it to tell you, using the print() function you already know. Print debugging means inserting print statements at the points in your code where you suspect something has gone wrong, running the program, and reading the output to see what values variables actually hold, as opposed to what you assumed they held.

This is the simplest way to make the debugging process from the previous chapter concrete. Debugging asks you to form a hypothesis about the cause of a bug and then test it; print debugging is one of the most common ways to test that hypothesis, since it requires no special setup, works in any environment that can run your code, and takes seconds to add.

A print statement used for debugging should show both the name of the variable and its value, not just the value by itself. print(largest) tells you a number changed, but not which variable it came from or at what point in the code; print(f"largest={largest}") tells you exactly what you are looking at, which matters once you have several print statements scattered through a function.

Here is a function that is supposed to find the largest number in a list:

def find_max(numbers):
    largest = 0
    for n in numbers:
        if n > largest:
            largest = n
    return largest

Calling find_max([-5, -2, -8]) returns 0, which is not even in the list. To find out why, add a print statement inside the loop: print(f"n={n}, largest={largest}"). Running the function now prints n=-5, largest=0, then n=-2, largest=0, then n=-8, largest=0. The value of largest never changes, which immediately reveals the bug: largest starts at 0, and since every number in this list is negative, the condition n > largest is never true. The fix is to initialize largest to the first element of the list, numbers[0], instead of assuming 0 is always a safe starting point.

Print debugging has real limits, though. It clutters your code with statements you have to remember to remove or comment out later. It only shows you the values you thought to print, at the moment you thought to print them, so if the bug turns out to be somewhere you did not add a print statement, you have to add more, rerun, and repeat. It also cannot pause execution: the program runs straight through, dumping all its output at once, which becomes unwieldy inside a loop that runs a thousand times when you only care about iteration 47. That last limitation is exactly what dedicated debugger tools are built to solve.
